title: Numerical simulation of a two-frequency-driven superlattice Faraday-wave pattern
authors: Debashis Panda, Nicolas Périnet, Abdullah M. Abdal, Lyes Kahouadji, Seungwon Shin, Jalel Chergui, Damir Juric, Omar K. Matar, Laurette S. Tuckerman
abstract: The formation of a superlattice pattern in two-frequency-driven Faraday waves discovered and named SSS-I by Arbell & Fineberg (1998, 2002) is investigated by means of Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) of the full three-dimensional Navier--Stokes equations with a free surface. Two simulations with distinct quasi-hexagonal initial conditions run at a forcing amplitude $25\%$ above the Faraday-wave onset followed quite different routes, but both led eventually to the same superlattice pattern after around 250 forcing periods. This regime is inaccessible to the approximations of weak nonlinearity or viscosity. The standing-wave pattern contain rows of patches, alternating in time between hills and lakes that are connected by a long skeleton resembing the backbone of DNA strands. The patches and skeleton of the pattern can be related to its spatial Fourier decomposition, which combines hexagonal modes with a spatially and temporally subharmonic mode. One of the transition routes passes through several fairly long-lived transients including different hexagonal patterns and another superlattice pattern; the other passes only through erratic and disordered states. After another 100 periods, the pattern became unstable and was succeeded by a dynamic version of SSS-I in which the superlattice is modulated and drifts in the direction of the backbone, while preserving its basic shape. Convergence to SSS-I states both experimentally in a large geometry and numerically from two different initial conditions and in a minimal geometry demonstrates the robustness of the SSS-I pattern.
summary: This paper uses advanced numerical simulations to study the complex formation of a superlattice pattern (SSS-I) in Faraday waves driven by two frequencies. The authors demonstrate that this pattern is highly robust, converging reliably even from different starting conditions. The work highlights the necessity of solving the full Navier-Stokes equations because simpler theoretical approximations fail in this highly nonlinear regime.
main_problem: The study investigates the formation and dynamics of a superlattice Faraday-wave pattern (SSS-I) driven by two distinct frequencies.
main_result: The SSS-I superlattice pattern is robustly formed, converging from different initial conditions, and can transition into a dynamic, drifting version while maintaining its basic structure.
method: The research employs Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) solving the full three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations, supplemented by theoretical analysis of mode interactions and symmetry conditions.
model_or_system: The physical system is a fluid layer subjected to two-frequency vertical oscillation (Faraday waves). The dynamics are modeled using the full 3D Navier-Stokes equations for a free surface interface.
key_observables: The superlattice pattern itself (patches connected by a 'backbone'), its spatial Fourier decomposition (hexagonal and subharmonic modes), and the temporal evolution of mode amplitudes.
important_parameters: Two-frequency forcing parameters ($\mathbf{F}$), forcing amplitude relative to onset ($25\%$ above), and simulation time (requiring $\sim 250$ forcing periods for convergence).
main_assumptions: The simulations are performed in regimes where weak nonlinearity or viscosity approximations fail, necessitating the use of the full Navier-Stokes equations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental SSS-I pattern, its spatial Fourier spectrum showing hexagonal and subharmonic modes, and diagrams detailing the computational domain setup and mode evolution.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical model and the necessity of full DNS, through demonstrating the convergence to the stable SSS-I state from multiple initial conditions, and concluding with analyses of pattern stability and symmetry breaking via mode analysis.
why_interesting: While focused on fluid dynamics, the study of pattern formation, stability transitions, and the role of multiple interacting modes (like the subharmonic mode) shares mathematical parallels with pattern formation in nonlinear wave systems relevant to AMO physics or open quantum systems.
